lessons.t: Where coding agents run: IDE assistants, terminal agents, background and cloud agents
lessons.html:
Every coding tool now runs the same agent loop from Chapter 6: read the code, plan, edit, run a command, read the result, repeat. What separates the products is where that loop runs, how long it runs before a human looks, and what the human sees when it stops. Sort tools by those three things and the vendor list stops being confusing.

ShapeExamples (as of October 2026)Where the loop runsWho waits for whomBest for
IDE assistantGitHub Copilot in VS Code, Cursor, the Claude Code and Codex IDE extensionsOn the developer’s machine, inside the editorThe agent waits for the developer after every diffEdits the developer understands and wants to steer line by line
Terminal agentClaude Code CLI, Codex CLI, Google’s Antigravity CLIOn the developer’s machine, with shell accessThe developer approves actions according to permission settings, or lets it runMulti-file changes, running tests, debugging, scripted work in CI
Background or cloud agentClaude Code on the web, Codex cloud, Cursor cloud agents, GitHub Copilot’s cloud agentIn an isolated cloud environment with the repo clonedThe developer assigns a task and comes back to a branch or pull requestWell-specified tasks that can run in parallel while people do other work
Review and CI agentCopilot code review, Claude Code GitHub Actions and Code Review, Codex code review, Cursor BugbotIn the pipeline, triggered by repo eventsNobody waits; it comments or opens a PRFirst-pass review, triage, scheduled maintenance

Three things are true across the market as of October 2026.

  • Every major vendor spans every shape. Anthropic documents one Claude Code engine behind its terminal, IDE, desktop, web and Slack surfaces. Google moved consumer users from Gemini CLI to Antigravity CLI in June 2026, and says the CLI shares its harness with the Antigravity desktop app. Cursor renamed Background Agents to cloud agents and lets you start them from Slack, Linear, GitHub comments or an API. Picking a vendor no longer picks a shape.
  • The configuration layer is converging. AGENTS.md, a Markdown file of project conventions that started in OpenAI’s Codex tooling, was contributed to the Linux Foundation’s Agentic AI Foundation in December 2025, alongside MCP. Claude Code, Copilot, Cursor and others read it. Repo instructions, MCP servers, skills and hooks are increasingly portable, so switching cost sits elsewhere.
  • The real switching cost is the environment. A cloud agent is only as good as its ability to install dependencies, build, run tests and reach the services it needs. Each vendor configures this differently (a setup workflow, a snapshot, a Dockerfile). Teams that invest here get far more out of background agents.

Hard limits are product facts

Each tool has constraints that shape which tasks you can delegate. GitHub documents that a Copilot cloud agent task works in one repository, on one branch, produces one pull request, and runs for at most 59 minutes. Cursor bills cloud agents at API pricing with a spend limit. Read these pages before you promise a workflow, and recheck them quarterly.

What to evaluate

Run the bake-off method from Chapter 3 on your own backlog, and score each tool on: whether the agent can build and test your repo unaided; the permission model and where secrets live; the quality of session logs a reviewer can read; how work comes back (diff, branch, PR with evidence such as test output or screenshots); and the cost model at your expected volume.

What changes for you

  • Describe AI coding work in your plans by shape (IDE, terminal, cloud, CI). The shape decides who waits and who reviews, whichever vendor you use.
  • Fund environment setup for cloud agents as real engineering work, with an owner. It is the main predictor of whether background agents produce mergeable PRs.
  • Put each tool’s hard limits (session length, repo scope, spend caps) in the team playbook and review them every quarter, since they change often.

lessons.t: More code is not more software: review and integration become the bottleneck
lessons.html:
Coding agents make writing a first draft of code much cheaper. Shipping software involves much more than drafting: deciding what to build, reviewing, integrating, testing, deploying and owning the result. When one stage gets faster, the queue moves to the next one. The evidence so far is consistent with that.

What the primary research shows

  • Perceived speed and measured speed can diverge. In METR’s early-2025 randomised trial, 16 experienced open-source developers worked on 246 real tasks in repos they knew well. With AI tools allowed, tasks took about 19% longer, yet developers believed afterwards that AI had sped them up. METR’s February 2026 follow-up could not produce a clean new estimate: many developers refused to work without AI, withheld tasks they did not want to do by hand, and ran several agents at once, which broke time tracking. METR believes developers were likely more sped up in early 2026 than in early 2025, and calls its own data very weak evidence of the size.
  • Passing tests is not the same as mergeable. In METR’s August 2025 study on 18 issues from two mature open-source repos, an agent passed the maintainers’ tests about 38% of the time. Of 15 PRs reviewed by hand, none was mergeable as-is. Every one had at least three of five problem types: core functionality, test coverage, documentation, linting and formatting, other code quality. Fixing them took reviewers an estimated 42 minutes on average, roughly a third of the original human time.
  • Throughput rises, and so does instability. The 2025 DORA report (nearly 5,000 respondents, 90% using AI) found AI adoption now associated with higher delivery throughput and with higher delivery instability. DORA describes AI as an amplifier of existing strengths and dysfunctions. A March 2026 DORA analysis names a verification tax: time saved writing is spent auditing, and large AI-authored changes raise reviewers’ cognitive load.

Secondary statistics

You will see figures claiming agents raise code output by a fixed percentage with no gain in finished work, or that review times have doubled. Most come from vendor telemetry that is hard to audit and defines terms differently. The direction matches DORA and METR. Quote the primary studies in planning documents, and measure your own pipeline.

Why the bottleneck moves

Apply Amdahl’s law to delivery. In an illustrative team where writing code is 25% of the time from ticket to production, an infinitely fast code writer caps the end-to-end speedup at 1.33×. The other 75% (clarifying intent, review, CI, integration, release, fixing what broke) sets the pace, and cheap code adds load to several of those stages.

StageWhat happens when drafting is cheapSignal to watch
Deciding what to buildMore options get built; ambiguity surfaces later, in reviewPRs rejected for intent, not code
ReviewMore and larger PRs per reviewer; reviewers skimReview wait time, PR size, approvals with no comments
CI and testMore runs, flaky tests block more workQueue time, flake rate
IntegrationParallel agent branches conflictMerge conflicts, reverted PRs
ProductionDefects escape faster than they are caughtChange failure rate, incidents per deploy

The useful response is to raise the capacity of the constrained stages: small batches, tests that run fast, review agents as a first pass, and specs that settle intent before code exists (next lesson).

What changes for you

  • Stop reporting lines of code, PR counts or “percentage of code written by AI” as success metrics. Report lead time from ticket to production, review wait time and change failure rate, before and after.
  • When a team adopts agents, plan explicit capacity for review and integration. Treat reviewer hours as the scarce resource in sprint planning.
  • Ask for a cap on PR size for agent-authored work. Small changes keep review honest.

lessons.t: Spec-driven development: the spec as the agent’s input
lessons.html:
A human engineer who gets a vague ticket asks questions, reads the history and pushes back. An agent fills the gaps with plausible guesses and delivers working code that does the wrong thing. That failure shows up in review, the most expensive place to discover it. Spec-driven development moves the clarification earlier: a written spec, then a plan, then tasks, then code, with a human checkpoint between each.

Two public examples show the pattern. GitHub’s open-source Spec Kit runs Spec → Plan → Tasks → Implement, each step producing a Markdown file that feeds the next, and works with most major coding agents. AWS’s Kiro produces requirements.md, design.md and tasks.md, with review gates between them, plus a quick mode that skips the gates. The pattern works with any agent and a folder of Markdown files.

Three layers of agent input

LayerLives inChangesOwner
Standing contextAGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md, skills, lintersRarelyEngineering lead
Feature specA spec file in the repo, linked from the ticketPer featurePM for what and why; engineer for constraints
TaskThe prompt or issue the agent receivesPer runWhoever delegates the task

Standing context is Chapter 4’s context engineering applied to a repo. The feature spec is where PMs add the most value.

What a feature spec for an agent contains

  • Problem and user outcome in two or three sentences.
  • Acceptance criteria written as checks a test or a reviewer can verify: inputs, expected behaviour, edge cases. This is Chapter 5’s eval mindset applied to code.
  • Non-goals and constraints: what not to touch, performance budgets, data that must not leave a boundary.
  • Interfaces: API shapes, events, UI states, error states.
  • Verification: the command that proves it works, and what evidence the PR must include (test output, screenshots).
  • Definition of done covering the categories agents miss: tests, docs, lint and types, observability.

Size the spec to the blast radius

A one-hour bug fix needs ten lines in the issue. A multi-day feature touching payments needs a reviewed spec and a reviewed plan before any code. A rule that works: if a wrong guess would cost more than a day of rework, a human approves the plan first.

Where it goes wrong

  • Specs that rot. Once code ships, the spec drifts. Either keep it in the repo and update it in the same PR as the behaviour change, or mark it as historical.
  • Pseudo-code specs. Dictating implementation removes the agent’s advantage and your engineers’ judgement. Specify behaviour and constraints.
  • Waterfall by stealth. A 20-page spec for a feature nobody has tried is a guess. Prototype first (next lesson), then spec what you learned.

What changes for you

  • Write acceptance criteria as numbered, checkable statements an agent can turn into tests. Ask engineering to reject agent PRs that do not map to them.
  • For work above a set blast radius, add a plan-review step to the workflow. Ten minutes reading a plan saves hours in review.
  • Keep specs in the repo next to the code, so both agents and people read the current version.

lessons.t: PMs who build: prototyping and internal tools with agents
lessons.html:
A PM with a terminal agent can now build in an afternoon what used to need a sprint: a clickable prototype on real data, a script that answers a usage question, an eval harness, a small internal tool. That changes how fast you can learn. It also creates a new way to cause damage, because a prototype that works in a demo looks finished to everyone who did not build it.

What you buildWhy it paysMain riskRule
Throwaway prototypeTests a flow with users before engineering commitsStakeholders treat it as nearly doneLabel it, give it an expiry date, never deploy it to customers
Data or analysis scriptAnswers questions without waiting for an analystWrong joins produce confident wrong numbersHave a second person or a second method check any number that drives a decision
Eval harness (Chapter 5)Lets you run and read your own evals weeklyLow, if it only reads dataKeep it in the team repo so engineers can run it too
Internal toolRemoves a manual workflowBecomes production with no ownerOnce three or more people depend on it, hand it to engineering with a spec, or retire it
Bug reproductionTurns a vague report into a failing testLowAttach it to the ticket

How to work

  • Start in a sandbox. A separate repo or branch, read-only copies of data, no production credentials. Chapter 12 covers why agents with secrets and untrusted input are dangerous.
  • Ask for a plan before code. Read it. Most agents have a planning mode or will plan if asked.
  • Work in small steps and commit often, so you can roll back when the agent goes down a bad path.
  • Make the agent prove it works. Ask it to write tests and run them, and to show you the output. Click through it yourself.
  • Ask it to explain the code. You are going to be asked how it works. If you cannot answer, you do not own it.

The demo gap

A prototype answers “could this work?”. Production also needs authentication, permissions, error states, accessibility, scale, monitoring and someone to fix it at 2am. METR’s finding that test-passing agent code still needed substantial work before merge (previous lesson) applies to your prototypes too. The lab at the end of this chapter measures that gap on your own build.

Handing over

When a prototype earns a place on the roadmap, hand engineering three things: the spec (written after the prototype, from what users did), the prototype as a reference for behaviour, and a list of known gaps. Do not hand over the prototype’s code as the starting point unless the engineers choose to use it. This keeps the conversation on what to build, which is your job, and leaves how to build it with them.

Building also changes your relationship with engineers. A PM who brings a working prototype to a planning meeting shifts the debate from opinions to evidence. A PM who bypasses review to ship an internal tool to customers loses trust quickly. Agree the boundary with your engineering lead before you start.

What changes for you

  • Prototype before you spec for anything with an uncertain user flow. Bring the prototype to user tests, not to stakeholder reviews as a promise.
  • Agree a written boundary with engineering: what PMs may build, where it may run, and the trigger for hand-off.
  • Put an expiry date on every prototype and internal tool you build. Delete or hand off on that date.

lessons.t: Governance: tracing, permissions and code quality over time
lessons.html:
Treat a coding agent as a fast, tireless contributor with no memory of last week and no stake in the outcome. Governance answers three questions about that contributor: what did it do, what was it allowed to do, and is the codebase getting better or worse because of it.

Tracing: what did it do?

Every serious tool now produces a record. GitHub’s cloud agent keeps session logs that teammates with repo access can follow. Cursor cloud agent runs have shareable URLs with screenshots, videos and logs. Claude Code exports OpenTelemetry metrics and events, including lines changed, commits, pull requests, cost, tokens, and each accept or reject decision on a tool call; prompt content is redacted unless an admin turns it on. Use these records for three jobs:

  • Review. A reviewer should see the task, the plan, the commands run and the test output alongside the diff.
  • Attribution. Label agent-authored PRs or commits (most tools add a co-author trailer). You cannot measure quality by source without it.
  • Cost and adoption. Spend per merged PR is more honest than spend per seat.

Permissions: what was it allowed to do?

  • Least privilege. Agents get scoped tokens, allow and deny lists for commands, restricted network egress and no production secrets. Cloud agent products let you restrict outbound domains and inject secrets per environment.
  • Branch protection applies to agents. GitHub documents that rulesets can block its agent; admins must choose to add it as a bypass actor. Do not.
  • A human merges. An agent may open and update PRs. Merging to protected branches stays with a named person, except for categories the team has explicitly automated (for example, lockfile updates that pass CI).
  • Untrusted input. An agent that reads issues, web pages or dependencies can be prompt-injected. Chapter 12 covers the threat model.

Quality over time

The risk is slow decay that no single PR reveals.

RiskSignalControl
Duplication and sprawlNew helpers that copy existing ones; rising file countsStanding context naming shared modules; duplicate detection in CI
Circular verificationThe same agent writes the code and the only testsAcceptance tests derived from the spec; a human or second agent writes or reviews tests
Oversized PRsMedian PR size rising after agent adoptionSize caps; split large tasks in the plan
Comprehension debtNobody can explain a module in a design reviewRequire the author to walk through the change; rotate ownership
Rubber-stamp reviewApprovals with no comments, faster than a person can readReview agents for style and obvious bugs, humans for design and intent

DORA’s March 2026 guidance points the same way: give authors AI feedback while they write, use context-aware review agents before human review, work in small batches and invest in fast test automation.

What changes for you

  • Require attribution of agent-authored changes, so you can compare defect and revert rates by source each quarter.
  • Write permissions for agents into the team playbook: which commands, which secrets, which branches, who merges.
  • Add two quality trends to your quarterly engineering review: median PR size and reverts or incidents traced to agent-authored changes.

lessons.t: Where it’s heading: longer autonomous runs, agents in CI, smaller teams
lessons.html:
Predictions about AI coding age badly. The useful habit is to name the trends, the evidence for each as of now, and the signal that would change your plan. Revisit this lesson every quarter.

Longer autonomous runs

METR measures a model’s time horizon: the length of task, in skilled-human time, that a model completes with 50% reliability. Its page, last updated in September 2026, reports that an exponential trend still fits the data better than any curve that flattens. Read it with three caveats: 50% is a capability bar, far from the reliability a product needs (Chapter 3 on pass^k); tasks are mostly software, ML and security; and METR flags measurements above about 16 hours as unreliable with its current task suite. Usage data points the same way. Anthropic reported in February 2026 that the 99.9th-percentile Claude Code turn nearly doubled between October 2025 and January 2026, from under 25 minutes to over 45, while the median turn stayed around 45 seconds. Most work is still short and interactive. The tail is getting long.

Agents in CI and on schedules

Agents are moving from a developer’s session into the pipeline: review on every PR, triage of new issues and failing builds, routines that run on a schedule or on repository events, and agentic workflows defined in the repo. Work no one asked for in a chat window arrives as PRs. That raises the stakes on the governance in the previous lesson, since nobody watched the run.

Smaller teams

The claim that AI lets a few people do the work of many is common. The evidence is thin and mixed. DORA’s finding that AI amplifies existing strengths and weaknesses suggests strong teams gain most. Plan for changed roles before fewer roles: more time on specs, review, evals and integration (Chapter 14).

TrendEvidence as of October 2026What to do nowWhat would change your plan
Longer runsMETR time horizons still on an exponential fit; long tail of agent turns growingPilot multi-hour tasks on low-risk work with strong testsAgent PRs from long runs merging with little rework
Agents in CIVendor support for event-triggered and scheduled agents across major toolsStart with review comments and triage, which change no codeLow false-positive rate on review comments over a quarter
Parallel agentsDesktop and cloud tools manage many sessions at onceCap concurrent agent PRs per reviewerReview capacity, not agent capacity, limiting throughput
Smaller teamsAnecdote and self-report; no strong causal studiesMeasure lead time and quality before changing headcount plansCredible studies showing delivery gains at constant quality

Re-evaluation trigger

Rerun the Chapter 3 bake-off on your own backlog when any major lab ships a new coding model or harness, or every quarter, whichever comes first. Track one number: the share of delegated tasks that merge with less than 30 minutes of human rework (an illustrative threshold; set your own).

What changes for you

  • Put an AI coding review on the quarterly calendar: rerun the bake-off, update tool limits in the playbook, and revisit which task types you delegate.
  • Start agents in CI with read-only work (review comments, triage) and widen scope only when the false-positive rate is acceptable.
  • In headcount and roadmap discussions, ask for lead time and change failure rate data before accepting a productivity assumption.

lab.title: Ship a prototype in a day, then price the hardening
lab.time: one working day plus a 90-minute review
lab.intro: This lab measures, on your own code, the gap between a working prototype and something your team would merge. The output is a real hardening ratio you can use in planning, in place of a guess.
steps: Pick the task. Choose an internal tool or prototype a real user wants, small enough for one day: one or two screens, one data source, no payments or personal data. Write down who will use it.
Write a one-page spec. Problem, user outcome, 8–12 numbered acceptance criteria written as checks, non-goals, and the command that proves it works. Time how long the spec takes.
Build with a coding agent in a sandbox. Separate repo or branch, read-only data, no production credentials. Timebox to four hours. Ask for a plan first, then build in small committed steps.
Log every intervention. Each time you correct, redirect or rescue the agent, note the time, the reason (missing context, wrong approach, bug, slow or stuck) and minutes spent.
Test against the spec. Run every acceptance criterion yourself. Record pass or fail. Put it in front of the intended user for 15 minutes.
Get a production review. Ask an engineer to review it as if it were a PR to your main product, using the rubric below. They estimate the hours to make it mergeable in each category.
Compute the ratio. Hardening ratio = estimated hardening hours ÷ build hours. Note which categories dominate.
Decide and write up. Keep, hand off, or delete. Write half a page on what you would delegate to an agent next time, what needs a tighter spec, and what the ratio means for planning.
lab.template:
CategoryPasses as-is? (Y/N)Issues foundHours to fix (engineer estimate)
Core functionality against acceptance criteria
Test coverage
Documentation and code comments
Linting, formatting and types
Other code quality (duplication, structure)
Security and permissions
Error states and accessibility
Observability and operations
Totals: build hours, hardening hours, ratio
lab.done: You have a working prototype a real user has tried, an intervention log, a reviewed rubric with hour estimates, and a hardening ratio. You can say which categories agents handled well on your codebase and which needed people, with numbers from your own team.

quiz.q: After a team adopts coding agents, PR count per engineer is up sharply but lead time from ticket to production is flat. What is the most likely explanation?
o: The agents are generating incorrect code that fails CI
The constraint has moved to review, integration and release, which did not get faster
Engineers are using the agents wrong and need training
PR count is the wrong unit; lines of code would show the gain
quiz.w: Faster drafting moves the queue to the next stage. DORA and METR both point to verification and review as the new constraint, so measure and add capacity there.

quiz.q: An agent’s PR passes all existing tests. Based on METR’s 2025 holistic evaluation study, what should a reviewer still expect?
o: Nothing; passing maintainer tests means it is mergeable
Only formatting issues that a linter will fix
Gaps in test coverage, documentation and code quality that still take meaningful human time
Security vulnerabilities in most cases
quiz.w: In METR’s study none of the reviewed agent PRs was mergeable as-is, and even test-passing runs averaged around 26 minutes of fixes, mostly coverage, docs and quality.

quiz.q: You want to delegate a two-day feature that touches billing to a cloud agent. What is the best first step?
o: Write a spec with checkable acceptance criteria, have the agent produce a plan, and get an engineer to approve the plan before implementation
Assign the issue to the agent and review the PR when it arrives
Write detailed pseudo-code so the agent cannot deviate
Split it into 20 tiny issues and assign them all at once
quiz.w: A wrong guess here costs more than a day of rework, so clarify intent before code exists. Pseudo-code removes judgement, and parallel tiny issues create integration conflicts.

quiz.q: A PM built a popular internal dashboard with a coding agent. Twelve people now use it daily and it reads production data. What should happen?
o: Keep maintaining it personally, since it works
Open it to customers because users like it
Hand it to engineering with a spec and known gaps, or retire it
Ask the agent to add more features so it is complete
quiz.w: Once several people depend on a tool it is production software and needs an owner, review and permissions. The PM’s build becomes a reference for engineering.

quiz.q: Which governance rule for agent-authored code is most important to keep?
o: Agents may merge to main if CI passes
Agents are added as bypass actors on branch rulesets so they are not blocked
Agent PRs skip review to save reviewer time
A named human merges to protected branches, apart from categories the team has explicitly automated
quiz.w: The agent can open and update PRs, but accountability for merging stays with a person. Bypassing rulesets removes the protection the rules exist to provide.

quiz.q: A vendor slide says agents now complete hours-long tasks. How should you read METR’s time-horizon trend when planning?
o: As the reliability you can expect in production
As a 50%-success capability measure on mostly software tasks, which needs your own tests at the reliability your product requires
As proof that teams can shrink this year
As irrelevant, because benchmarks do not measure coding
quiz.w: Time horizon is set at 50% success. Products need far higher reliability, so it signals direction, and your own bake-off decides what to delegate.

deliverable.title: Team playbook for agent-written code
deliverable.html:
One page your team agrees and revisits each quarter. Fill in each section with your own rules and thresholds.

  1. Task tiers. Three tiers by blast radius (for example: docs and tests; contained feature work; anything touching auth, payments, data or infrastructure). For each, the shapes allowed (IDE, terminal, cloud, CI) and whether a plan must be approved first.
  2. Who specs. What a task, a feature spec and standing context must contain. Where specs live. Who owns AGENTS.md.
  3. Who reviews. Review agent first pass, then a named human. Maximum PR size for agent-authored changes. Evidence required in the PR: test output, screenshots, link to the session log.
  4. What gets merged. Who may merge, which categories are auto-merged after CI, and the rule that agents never bypass branch protection.
  5. Permissions. Allowed commands, network egress, secrets per environment, and what agents never touch.
  6. PMs who build. Where PM prototypes may run, their expiry date, and the hand-off trigger.
  7. Measures. Lead time, review wait time, change failure rate and reverts, split by agent-authored and human-authored, reviewed quarterly.
  8. Tool limits and review date. Each tool’s session, scope and spend limits as of the date written, and the date of the next review.

Sign-off: engineering lead, product lead, and security for the permissions section.
